header: DB-backed designation/rank layer. It replaces the old hardcoded RANKS[] / HIERARCHY[] arrays in designations.ts entirely: every title, code, track and rank_order value comes from `public.designation_grade` (30 rows, built in the Stage 8 SAIL seniority project), never hardcoded here. Confirmed live (chat, 28 Sep 2026):

- "Asst. Manager" appears at BOTH code 204 (paired with Medical Officer) and code 201 (paired with Junior Manager): two real, distinct grades (rank_order 12 and 13) that happen to share one display title. A bare, unqualified "Asst Manager" search combines both grade ids. Each person's own designation_grade_id already correctly records which one they actually are; search just needs to not miss either.
- "Director In-charge" (code 227, rank_order 1) is a real title the old hardcoded RANKS array never had at all.

doc: Typed shorthand -> the EXACT stored title it means. I keep this separate from the DB so a stored title can have several typable spellings without a migration per spelling. It is carried forward from the old RANKS aliases (already validated over many prior sessions), plus the two fixes found in this session: "officer(s)" for exec, "non-ex"/"nonex"/"non ex" for non-exec. These were previously only in resolveDesignation(), never in the routing matcher, which is exactly why they mis-routed to circular search (see chat).

symbols.returns: Promise<{ term: string; resolution: DesignationResolution } | null>
doc: Find a designation term ANYWHERE in free text (word-bounded, not position-anchored): "in c&it list executives" and "list executives in c&it" must both match. The longest known phrase wins. parser.ts uses this to decide routing. It replaces the old findDesignation() and its hand-rolled regex set (which is what was missing "officer"/"non-ex" and caused the mis-routing).

doc: True only when the ENTIRE phrase is nothing but a recognised designation term (plus its own plural). I use it to tell "for employees" apart from a genuine department name (see parser.ts's findDeptScope).
